title: CASE OF SULEJMANOV v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
conclusion: No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Procedural aspect)
summary: In the case of Sulejmanov v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicant, Mr. Sulejmanov, identified as a member of the Roma community, brought a complaint against the state concerning his treatment by police. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police brutality and the lack of effective investigations into such allegations, a persistent issue for these communities across Europe. On 13 March 1998, Mr. Sulejmanov and a friend, both of Roma origin, were stopped by police near the village of Balvan on suspicion of theft. According to Mr. Sulejmanov, they were immediately beaten by police officers, subjected to racist insults, and further assaulted at the police station, where they were denied water and left tied up overnight. After his release, Mr. Sulejmanov sought medical attention for a broken arm, but his injuries were not properly documented due to financial constraints and the use of a relative’s identity card. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court found no substantive violation of Article 3, as it could not be established beyond reasonable doubt that the police had inflicted the injuries. However, it found a procedural violation, ruling that the authorities had failed to conduct an effective investigation into Mr. Sulejmanov’s credible allegations of ill-treatment. This judgment is significant as it underscores the ongoing need for robust, impartial investigations into police violence against Roma and Travellers, reflecting broader concerns about systemic discrimination in the region during the late 1990s.
